client: I've been really struggling since my mom passed away six months ago. It feels like everyone around me has just... moved on with their lives, and I'm still stuck in this heavy fog that won't lift. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, but I didn't know what else to do.
therapist:
I'm really glad you reached out, even through the doubt — that took courage, and it tells me a part of you is still looking for a way through this. Losing your mom is one of the most profound losses a person can experience, and the fog you're describing makes complete sense; grief doesn't follow anyone else's timeline, no matter how much it might feel like it should. I'm here to move at whatever pace feels right for you, without any pressure.

Can you tell me a little more about what that "heavy fog" feels like for you day to day — is it more like sadness, numbness, exhaustion, or something harder to name?

client: It's kind of all of those things at once, which is part of what makes it so hard to explain to people. Like, I'll wake up and just feel this weight before I've even remembered why, and then it hits me again — oh right, she's gone. And then I feel guilty for those few seconds where I didn't remember, like I'm somehow betraying her by not carrying it every single moment.
therapist:
That guilt you're describing — feeling like forgetting, even for a moment, is a betrayal — is something so many grieving people experience, and it's such a painful extra layer on top of the loss itself. But I want to gently offer another way to look at it: those few seconds of not remembering aren't a sign that you love her less, they're simply your mind taking a brief, necessary breath. Your love for her isn't measured by how constantly you carry the pain.

What do you think she would say if she could see you feeling guilty for those moments?

client: I've thought about that before, actually — what she would say. And honestly, she'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself, because that's the kind of person she was. But knowing that doesn't really make the guilt go away, you know? It's like my head understands it, but my chest still feels like I'm doing something wrong every time I catch myself just... living.
therapist:
What you're describing - that gap between what your head knows and what your chest feels - is at the heart of so much of our suffering, and it's so real and valid that just "knowing better" doesn't automatically rewire that deep emotional response. It sounds like part of you has actually internalized a belief that continuing to live and even momentarily feel okay is somehow incompatible with loving her — and that's a thought worth gently examining together. She sounds like she was a truly compassionate person, and I wonder if the way you're speaking about her tells us something about the kind of love that actually existed between you.

When you imagine what it would look like to honor her memory *without* punishing yourself for living — even if it feels impossible right now — what comes up for you?

client: I sit with that question for a moment, and honestly, the first thing that comes up is just... blankness, like I can't even picture it. And then almost immediately this wave of guilt, like even trying to imagine it feels like a betrayal. I think part of me is scared that if I stop punishing myself, it means she didn't matter enough to me, even though I know that doesn't really make logical sense.
therapist:
That fear — that releasing the pain somehow equals releasing her — is one of the most common and heartbreaking traps grief can set for us, and the fact that you can already see it doesn't quite make logical sense shows real self-awareness. What your mind seems to have built is an equation: suffering equals love, so less suffering must mean less love — but that equation isn't true, even though it feels absolutely convincing right now. Grief and love aren't the same thing, and she can matter enormously to you even in your moments of peace.

I'm curious — can you think of any other relationship in your life where you'd measure someone's love for you by how much they suffered on your behalf?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. No, I wouldn't want someone to suffer for me to prove they love me — that actually sounds kind of awful when you put it that way. But it still feels different with my mom, like the rules are different when someone is gone and can't be here anymore.
therapist:
That moment of being stopped in your tracks is really important — you just caught your own mind applying a different, harsher set of rules to yourself than you would to anyone else you love, and that's a genuinely significant insight. It makes sense that it *feels* different when someone is gone, because the loss is so permanent and there's no more time to show her how much she meant to you in the ordinary ways — so the grief can start to feel like the only remaining proof of your love. But I wonder if there are other ways she already knew, and you already know, that didn't require your suffering.

What are some of the ways you showed her you loved her while she was still here?

client: I sat with that question for a second and it actually made my chest tighten up, which surprised me. I mean, I used to call her every Sunday without fail, and I'd drive two hours to take her to her doctor appointments because she hated going alone. But there's this voice in my head that immediately says "yeah, but that wasn't enough, you could have called more, visited more" — it just kind of cancels out whatever good I try to remember.
therapist:
The love in what you just described is so clear and so real — those Sunday calls, those two-hour drives — those aren't small things, those are devotion, and they speak volumes about who you were to her. But I want to gently name what just happened: the moment you accessed something true and good, that critical voice swooped in immediately to cancel it out, and I'd guess that voice has gotten very loud and very fast since she passed. That voice isn't the truth about you or your relationship — it sounds like it might be grief's way of keeping you locked in punishment mode.

If a close friend described doing all of those things for *their* mother, would that same voice tell you it still wasn't enough — or does it reserve that harshness specifically for you?

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because honestly... no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. If a friend told me they drove two hours every week and called every Sunday, I'd probably tell them they were a really good son or daughter. But when you put it that way, it almost makes it worse, because now I can see I'm holding myself to some impossible standard I'd never apply to anyone else, and I don't really know how to stop doing that.
therapist:
Seeing that double standard so clearly is actually a really meaningful breakthrough, even if it feels uncomfortable right now — awareness is genuinely the first step toward change, and you just did something hard and honest. That impossibly high standard didn't appear out of nowhere, and often these voices develop as a way of protecting us from something, so you don't need to pressure yourself to simply "stop" it overnight. The goal isn't to silence that voice through willpower, but to slowly, gently practice offering yourself the same compassion you'd so naturally give a friend.

If you were to speak to yourself about those Sunday calls and those long drives the way you'd speak to that friend — even just for a moment right now — what would you actually say?

client: I guess... I'd say something like, "You're doing what you can. You're showing up, even when it's hard, and that counts for something." But honestly, even just saying that out loud feels kind of hollow to me, like I'm just reciting words I don't actually believe yet — it doesn't feel the same as when I say it to someone else.
therapist:
The fact that it feels hollow right now is completely okay and actually really normal — you're essentially trying to speak a language your heart hasn't learned yet, and you can't expect fluency after just one sentence. What strikes me is that you *did* say it, even through the doubt, and that small act of trying matters more than whether it felt true in this moment. These things tend to start as words we recite before they slowly become things we actually feel, and that gap you're noticing isn't failure — it's just where you are right now in the process.

I'm wondering, is there a specific memory of a moment with your mom — maybe one of those Sunday calls or one of those drives — that when you picture it, even briefly makes you feel like you were genuinely there for her?

client: I guess... there was this one Sunday call, maybe six months before she passed, where she was telling me about this bird that kept coming to her feeder and she was so excited about it. I actually just listened for once, didn't try to fix anything or rush her off the phone, and she laughed at something I said and told me I always knew how to make her feel better. But then I think about how many other calls I cut short or half-listened to while I was doing something else, and that one good memory just gets swallowed up by all the guilt about the rest.
therapist:
That moment you just described — her laughing, telling you that you always knew how to make her feel better — that's not a small thing, that's her telling you exactly who you were to her, in her own words, unprompted. And I notice what happened just now: you held something genuinely beautiful for just a moment before that critical voice rushed in to bury it under everything else, which is exactly the pattern we've been seeing together today. The imperfect calls don't erase that moment, and that moment isn't an exception to who you were to her — it might actually be closer to the truth of your relationship than the guilt is.

What do you think it would feel like to let that memory of her laughing just exist for a little while, without immediately allowing the guilt to follow it in?

client: I want to say it would feel good, but honestly, the first thing I notice is this kind of... panic almost, like if I let myself just sit with that memory without the guilt attached, I'm somehow letting myself off the hook for all the times I wasn't there. It's like the guilt has become this weird way of proving that I loved her, you know? If I stop feeling bad, maybe it means I didn't care enough.
therapist:
You just articulated something really profound — that the guilt has become a way of keeping your love for her alive and visible, almost like it's the last thread connecting you to her, and letting it go feels like losing her all over again. That makes so much sense, and it also helps me understand why simply "thinking differently" hasn't been enough, because this isn't really about logic — it's about fear of losing your connection to her. But I want to offer a gentle thought: that memory of her laughing, the bird at the feeder, her voice saying you always made her feel better — that *is* her, and that connection lives in you in a way that guilt could never protect or replace.

What if the guilt isn't actually keeping you close to her — what do you think might happen to that connection if you leaned into the memory of her laughing instead?
